questions.problem: Which of the following gives the area bounded by graph of the polar curve $r=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta )$ for $\frac{2\pi }{3}\le \theta \le \pi ?$
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta )$, ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{2\pi }{3}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{\pi }{(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 9{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )$ for $\pi \le \theta \le \frac{5\pi }{4},$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )$, ${\theta }_{1}=\pi $ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{5\pi }{4}$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi }^{5\pi /4}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{25}{2}{\int }_{\pi }^{5\pi /4}{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{25}{4}{\int }_{\pi }^{5\pi /4}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{25}{4}(\theta {|}_{\pi }^{5\pi /4}+\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta ){|}_{\pi }^{5\pi /4}) \\  & =\frac{25}{4}((\frac{5\pi }{4}-(\pi ))+\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\pi ))) \\  & =\frac{25}{4}(\frac{\pi }{4}+0) \\  & =\frac{25\pi }{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{6}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{3}$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{4}\theta \,{|}_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}-\frac{9}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}(\frac{\pi }{3}-\frac{\pi }{6})-\frac{9}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})) \\  & =\frac{9}{4}\cdot \frac{\pi }{6}-\frac{9}{8}(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{8}-0 \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Area Bounded by the Loop of a Limaçon
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=4+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{6}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{6}$, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}(4+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}(16+16\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}(16+16\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(18\theta -16\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )){|}_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(18\theta \,{|}_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}-16\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}\,) \\  & =9\theta \,{|}_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}-8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6} \\  & =9(\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi }{6})-8(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{6}))-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{3})) \\  & =3\pi -8(0)-\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{3}) \\  & =3\pi -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the area $A$ bounded by the polar curve $r=5+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ for $\pi \le \theta \le 2\pi ,$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=5+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=\pi $ and ${\theta }_{2}=2\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(5+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(25+20\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(25+20\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(27\theta -20\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )){|}_{\pi }^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(27\theta \,{|}_{\pi }^{2\pi }-20\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi }^{2\pi }-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{\pi }^{2\pi }\,) \\  & =\frac{27}{2}\theta \,{|}_{\pi }^{2\pi }-10\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi }^{2\pi }-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{\pi }^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{27}{2}(2\pi -\pi )-10(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ))-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )) \\  & =\frac{27\pi }{2}-10(1-(-1))-\frac{1}{2}(0) \\  & =\frac{27\pi }{2}-20.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r=2-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ for $0\le \theta \le \pi ,$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=2-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(4-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi })) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{4}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =\frac{9}{4}\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{8}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{9}{4}(\pi -0)+2(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))-\frac{1}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{9\pi }{4}+2(-2)-\frac{1}{8}(0) \\  & =\frac{9\pi -16}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ ${\theta }_{1}=0,$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{2}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(\frac{3}{2}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{3}{2}\theta -2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{4}){|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{3}{2}\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{4}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }\,) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{8}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{3}{4}(\pi -0)-(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))+\frac{1}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}-0+0 \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}

questions.problem: Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r=3{e}^{2\theta }$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi .$
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=3{e}^{2\theta }$, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{(3{e}^{2\theta })}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{e}^{4\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{4}{e}^{4\theta }\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{9}{8}({e}^{4\pi }-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{9}{8}({e}^{4\pi }-1).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

When $r(\theta )=2{e}^{1-\theta }$, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}(2{e}^{1-\theta })^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}4{e}^{2-2\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{e}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}{e}^{-2\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{e}^{2}(-\frac{{e}^{-2\theta }}{2}){|}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)} \\  & =-{e}^{2}({e}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =-{e}^{2}(\frac{1}{9}-1) \\  & =\frac{8{e}^{2}}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r = \cos(3\theta)$ and the lines $\theta = -\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14060520/assets/350a721c254dab3a8acb2ae54ca5be0bcde6ab036e6936939194c57ae55fe4ff.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2(\theta) \, \textrm{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta) = \cos(3\theta),$ $\theta_1=-\dfrac{\pi}{6},$ and $\theta_2=\dfrac{\pi}{6},$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\theta {|}_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}+\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\theta ){|}_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}((\frac{\pi }{6}-(-\frac{\pi }{6}))+\frac{1}{6}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi ))) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\frac{\pi }{3}+0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

When $r(\theta) = 1+2\cos(\theta),$ $\theta_1=\dfrac{2\pi}{3},$ and $\theta_2=\dfrac{4\pi}{3},$ this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}(1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta ))^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}(1+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+4\cdot \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+2\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\pi -4\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\pi -3\sqrt{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding Areas Bounded by Other Polar Curves
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14060520/assets/d7b39805131dc562e233d49a84f69d30e80ca29cb9443012032d18fdb4512054.png)

Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r = 2\sin\theta + 2\cos\theta$ for $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{3\pi}{4},$ as shown above.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2(\theta) \, \textrm{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta) = 2\sin\theta + 2\cos\theta,$ $\theta_1=\dfrac{\pi}{2},$ and $\theta_2=\dfrac{3\pi}{4},$ this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}(4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +8\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}(4+8\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{4}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2(\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}) \\  & =2\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4} \\  & =2(\frac{3\pi }{4}-\frac{\pi }{2})-(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}-1 \\  & =\frac{\pi -2}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
